beginner: Celery is a marsh plant at heart, so it wants soil that stays damp and rich. Give it a loam or silt loam with lots of compost or rotted manure mixed in, the kind of soil that holds water without turning to swamp. Light, sandy soil is the hardest place to grow celery, because it dries out fast and celery hates drying out: that is what gives you stringy, bitter stalks. If your soil is sandy, dig in plenty of compost first, or grow celery in a raised bed or a big container with a moisture-holding mix. Celery is a heavy feeder, so a rich soil to start with makes the whole season easier.
seasoned: Celery descends from a wild marshland plant and performs best in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil high in organic matter, classically the muck and peat soils of commercial districts but in the home garden a well-amended loam or silt loam. Work in generous compost or well-rotted manure before planting, both to feed this heavy feeder and to hold the steady moisture celery demands. The texture priority is the opposite of its relative the carrot: where carrot wants a light, open, stone-free channel, celery wants water-holding capacity, since brief drying is what turns the petioles stringy, pithy, and bitter. Light sandy soils are the most difficult, drying too fast for celery's shallow roots; amend them heavily or switch to a raised bed. Reasonable drainage still matters, because waterlogged ground invites the pink rot and damping-off that plague this crop.

beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Celery likes it slightly acidic to near neutral, roughly 6.0 to 6.8. It is not extremely fussy, but very acidic soil can lock up calcium, and celery already struggles with calcium, that is what causes the black, dead centers called blackheart. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime before planting.
seasoned: Celery grows best in slightly acidic to near neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.8, and tolerates a band of about 5.8 to 7.0. Holding pH toward the upper end of that range matters more for celery than for most vegetables, because adequate calcium availability is central to preventing blackheart (the calcium-related death of the growing tip), and strongly acidic soil reduces calcium uptake. A standard extension soil test removes the guesswork and tells you whether lime is warranted before transplanting.

beginner: Celery is a hungry plant, the opposite of carrots. Mix lots of compost and a balanced fertilizer into the soil before you plant, then feed it again with a nitrogen fertilizer about every 3 to 4 weeks all season. The goal is to keep celery growing fast and without a pause. If it runs short of food or water, even for a while, the stalks turn tough, stringy, and bitter instead of crisp.
seasoned: Celery is a heavy feeder with a high nitrogen demand, the opposite of its low-nitrogen relative the carrot. Work plenty of compost or rotted manure plus a balanced fertilizer into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks through the season, on the order of a quarter cup of a high-nitrogen source such as 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row each application. Steady feeding and steady water together drive the fast, uninterrupted growth that produces tender stalks; any check from hunger or drought shows up as tough, stringy, bitter petioles.

beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Celery wants plenty of all three to start, like a 10-10-10, plus extra nitrogen (the first number) fed through the season. Mix compost in too. With celery you cannot easily overfeed the way you can with carrots: too little food is the bigger danger, because hungry celery grows tough and bitter.
seasoned: Celery is nitrogen-hungry and benefits from rich, steadily fed soil. Start with a balanced blend such as 10-10-10 worked in with compost at transplanting, then carry the crop with regular nitrogen side-dressings. Unlike root crops, celery will not fork or run to leaf from generous feeding: with celery the risk runs the other way, since underfeeding is a direct cause of stringy, bitter stalks. Keep calcium adequate as well, because calcium shortage, often triggered by uneven watering rather than truly low soil calcium, causes blackheart.

beginner: Mix a balanced vegetable fertilizer into the bed when you plant, with lots of compost, then feed again with a little nitrogen fertilizer every 3 to 4 weeks. A small handful of a high-nitrogen feed per few feet of row each time is plenty. Steady small feedings beat one big one.
seasoned: Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed at transplanting along with generous compost, then side-dress nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks, about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row each time (Utah State University Extension). Celery removes a lot of nitrogen over its long season, so err toward steady, repeated feeding rather than one heavy dose.

beginner: Celery is an easygoing neighbor that fits well among cabbage-family crops, bush beans, and onions or leeks, which many gardeners pair with it by tradition. The clearest plants to keep apart from celery are its own carrot-family relatives, carrot, parsnip, parsley, dill, and fennel, because they share the same pests and diseases. As always, treat most companion-planting charts with some skepticism, since many of their claims have not held up when tested.
seasoned: Celery slots easily into a mixed cool-season bed. The traditional pairings are with brassicas (cabbage, broccoli), bush beans, and alliums (onion, leek), all long-standing companion-planting lore rather than tested relationships, useful but not guaranteed. The best-grounded avoids are celery's own family, the Apiaceae: carrot, parsnip, parsley, dill, and fennel share its pest and disease spectrum (carrot rust fly, leaf blights, aster yellows), so clustering them concentrates that pressure. As with carrot, most companion-chart claims for celery rest on tradition rather than extension trials, so weight them accordingly.

beginner: Celery and cabbage-family plants are a classic old-time pairing. They like the same cool weather and rich, moist soil, so they make easy bed-mates. This is traditional garden wisdom rather than a tested rule, but it is harmless and convenient.
seasoned: Celery and the cabbage family share a culture, cool weather, rich soil, and steady moisture, so they make compatible neighbors, and the pairing is a fixture of traditional companion-planting guides. Treat the benefit as cultural compatibility and efficient bed use rather than a measured pest effect, since the relationship has not been demonstrated in controlled trials.

beginner: Bush beans are a traditional celery companion. Beans add some nitrogen to the soil, which suits hungry celery, and the two do not compete for the same space. A popular pairing, though more tradition than proven fact.
seasoned: The bean-celery pairing rests on the familiar legume rationale: beans fix nitrogen and are thought to share some with neighbors, which suits a nitrogen-hungry crop like celery. The in-season transfer is modest and not celery-specific in any controlled work, so treat this as traditional companion lore rather than a measured boost.

beginner: Onions, leeks, and other alliums are a traditional companion for celery, valued for their strong scent that some gardeners believe helps confuse pests. The evidence is thin, but they share a bed without trouble.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional aromatic companion, credited with masking the scent of neighboring crops from pests. The mechanism is the same one cited for the carrot-onion pairing and is plausible against the shared carrot rust fly, but it is not demonstrated for celery specifically. A harmless, space-sharing pairing best treated as tradition.

beginner: These are all celery's close cousins in the carrot family, and they catch the same pests and diseases, like the carrot rust fly and leaf blights. Growing them right next to celery lets those problems build up, so spread them around the garden instead.
seasoned: Carrot, parsnip, and parsley are fellow Apiaceae and share celery's pests and diseases, including carrot rust fly, the leaf blights, and aster yellows. Clustering the family concentrates that pressure, the same reason extension sources advise rotating related crops apart. Give each its own area rather than running them side by side.

beginner: Dill and fennel are also carrot-family relatives and share celery's pests. Fennel in particular is a poor neighbor to most vegetables, so keep both well away from your celery.
seasoned: Dill and fennel are carrot-family relatives that share celery's pest spectrum, and fennel additionally carries a near-universal reputation as a poor companion to most garden crops, attributed to root compounds that suppress neighbors. The lab work behind fennel's allelopathy targets weeds rather than celery, but between the shared pests and the tradition, the simple handling is to keep both well away from the celery bed.

beginner: You will see pale, squiggly trails winding through the leaves, like someone drew on them with a white pen. Those are tunnels made by tiny maggots feeding inside the leaf. Badly hit leaves look blotchy and dried out. A little is just cosmetic, but a lot weakens the plant.
seasoned: Pale, winding, snakelike tunnels (mines) trace through the leaf tissue, and heavier infestations leave leaves blotched, blistered, and partly dried. The damage is the larvae feeding between the upper and lower leaf surfaces; pinprick stippling on the foliage marks where adult females punctured leaves to feed and lay eggs. Light mining is cosmetic, but a heavy attack reduces the plant's vigor and the eating quality of the leafy tops.

beginner: The young (larvae) of small leafminer flies (Liriomyza). The adult fly lays eggs in the leaf, and the maggots that hatch tunnel around inside it. They like warm weather and attack lots of different plants. Tiny wasps usually keep them down on their own, unless heavy spraying kills off those helpers.
seasoned: Larvae of leafminer flies in the genus Liriomyza (notably Liriomyza trifolii and L. huidobrensis), small flies whose maggots mine within the leaf. Populations build in warm weather and can run through several overlapping generations; the pest also attacks many other vegetables and ornamentals, and natural enemies usually hold it in check unless broad-spectrum insecticides flare it up.

beginner: Lay a light row cover over young celery to keep the flies from laying eggs, keep the plants growing strongly, and let the natural helper insects do their job by not spraying. Check the leaves often, and pull off the first tunneled ones before they multiply.
seasoned: Cover young plants with floating row cover to exclude egg-laying adults, keep plants vigorous, and rely on conservation of natural enemies rather than spraying. Remove crop debris that can harbor pupae, and scout the leaves for the first stippling and mines so light infestations can be hand-removed before they build.

beginner: Tiny parasitic wasps usually keep leafminers in check. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays, which kill those helpers and often make outbreaks worse.
seasoned: Conserve the parasitic wasps that control leafminers; broad-spectrum insecticides flare this pest, so no chemical rung belongs here.

beginner: Little soft insects, usually green or gray, clustered on the newest leaves and in the crevices of the stalks, often leaving a sticky film. The bigger worry is that aphids spread a virus (celery mosaic) that yellows, mottles, and twists the leaves, which cannot be cured.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects, often green or gray, gather on the youngest growth and in the leaf and stalk crevices, leaving the plant sticky with honeydew that may turn black with sooty mold. Beyond direct feeding, aphids are the main concern as a vector: they transmit celery mosaic virus, which yellows, mottles, twists, and stunts the foliage with no cure.

beginner: Several kinds of aphids (small sap-sucking insects) feed on celery and multiply fast in mild weather. The main reason to care is that they carry a virus from plant to plant, so even a few can do harm beyond their feeding.
seasoned: Several aphid species colonize celery, including the bean aphid and foxglove aphid. They reproduce rapidly in mild weather and are spread further when winged forms move between plants; their role in moving celery mosaic virus from infected weeds and old celery makes even modest populations worth watching.

beginner: Keep weeds down and clear out old celery and carrot-family plants nearby, since they shelter aphids and the virus. Encourage natural helpers by not spraying harshly, and use a row cover on young plants. Reflective (silver) mulch helps keep aphids away where the virus is common.
seasoned: Control nearby weeds and remove old celery and carrot-family volunteers that host both aphids and the virus, use reflective mulch to deter colonizers where mosaic is a problem, and keep natural enemies active by minimizing insecticide use. Row cover protects young plants.

beginner: Aphids spread celery mosaic virus, so pull any plant with yellow, mottled, twisted leaves right away, and clear old celery and carrot-family weeds that host both.
seasoned: Remove mosaic-symptom plants promptly as virus reservoirs, and eliminate volunteer celery and carrot-family weeds that host aphids and the virus.

beginner: Rusty-brown tunnels and scars low on the stalks and roots, and weak or off-color plants when it is bad. It is the same pest that tunnels carrots, and it goes after celery too where it is common.
seasoned: Rusty-brown tunnels and scarring in the lower stalk bases and roots, sometimes with a rusty residue, and aboveground stunting or off-color foliage in heavier attacks. As a shared carrot-family pest, the same fly that mines carrots will work celery's crown and root zone where its populations are active.

beginner: The maggots of the carrot rust fly, a small fly that attacks the whole carrot family, including celery. The female lays eggs near the base of the plant and the maggots tunnel into the lower stalks and roots. It is mainly a problem in cool, damp, coastal areas.
seasoned: Larvae of the carrot rust fly (Psila rosae), whose females are drawn to the scent of carrot-family foliage and lay eggs near the crown; the maggots burrow into the lower stalks and roots. It is most damaging in cool, humid, maritime regions and far less of a problem in hot-summer areas.

beginner: A row cover laid over the bed and tucked in at the edges is the best defense, because the low-flying fly cannot reach the plants to lay eggs. Also keep celery away from where you grew carrots or parsnips last year, and do not plant it right next to them.
seasoned: Floating row cover sealed at the edges at planting is the most reliable home defense, since the low-flying females cannot reach the crowns. Rotate celery away from where carrot-family crops grew last year, and avoid planting it next to carrots or parsnips.

beginner: Seal the cover at the edges at planting. The fly flies low and cannot reach the crowns to lay eggs, which makes this the most reliable home defense.
seasoned: Edge-sealed row cover at planting is the most reliable home control, since the low-flying females cannot reach the crown.

beginner: Small yellow spots show up on both sides of the leaves, then grow into gray, round patches about a quarter inch to three quarters of an inch wide. As they spread the leaf turns papery and cracks. Unlike late blight, the stalks often stay fairly clean even when leaves are spotty. A badly blighted plant grows poorly.
seasoned: Small yellow spots appear on both surfaces of the leaves and enlarge into gray, roughly circular lesions about 1/4 to 3/4 inch across; as they multiply the tissue between them turns papery and often splits and cracks, and severe spotting blights the foliage. In contrast to late blight, the petioles often stay relatively clean even when the leaves are heavily spotted. Badly blighted plants size up poorly.

beginner: A fungus (Cercospora apii) that can ride in on the seed and survive on old celery debris. It likes warm weather, about 60 to 86°F, together with wet leaves from rain, dew, fog, or overhead watering. The spores spread in wind and splashing water.
seasoned: The fungus Cercospora apii, which is seedborne and also survives on celery debris in the field. It is favored by warm conditions, roughly 60 to 86°F, with leaf wetness from rain, dew, fog, or overhead irrigation; spores spread on wind and splashing water.

beginner: Use clean, tested seed and healthy transplants, do not grow celery (or its relatives) in the same spot two years running, clear away old debris, water at the soil in the morning, and give plants room so leaves dry fast. Stay out of the bed when the plants are wet.
seasoned: Start with disease-indexed (Cercospora-tested) seed and disease-free transplants, rotate celery and other carrot-family crops out of the bed for at least a year, clear crop debris, water at the base in the morning, and space plants for airflow. Avoid working among plants while the foliage is wet.

beginner: In a wet year a copper fungicide started early can slow spread. It does not cure leaves that are already spotted.
seasoned: A protectant copper, begun at first symptoms in wet weather, suppresses spread but does not cure infected tissue.

beginner: Small yellow spots on the leaves and stalks that enlarge, run together, and turn tan and papery, speckled with tiny dark dots (the telltale sign). Unlike early blight, this one spots the stalks too, which ruins the part you eat. It is usually the worse of the two blights.
seasoned: Small, discrete yellow spots appear on leaves and petioles and enlarge, often coalescing, then turn tan and dry to a papery texture; tiny dark fruiting bodies (pycnidia) speckle the lesions, the diagnostic sign that separates it from early blight. Unlike early blight, late blight readily lesions the stalks themselves, downgrading the harvest. It is usually the more damaging of the two celery blights.

beginner: A fungus (Septoria apiicola, not the same as potato or tomato late blight). It usually arrives on the seed and survives on old debris. It needs wet leaves and stops growing below about 55°F, getting worse above 70°F with rain, dew, fog, or overhead watering, which splash the spores around.
seasoned: The fungus Septoria apiicola (unrelated to the potato and tomato late blight). It is seedborne, the primary inoculum source, and survives on infected debris. Development stops below about 55°F and is favored above 70°F with leaf wetness from rain, heavy dew, fog, or sprinkler irrigation; splashing water disperses the spores.

beginner: The most important thing is to start with tested, clean seed, because the disease usually comes in on the seed. Use healthy transplants, water at the soil instead of overhead, do not grow celery in the same place two years in a row, clear away infected leftovers, and keep out of the bed when the plants are wet.
seasoned: The single most important step is Septoria-indexed (tested) seed, since seed is the main source; plant only disease-free transplants, avoid overhead sprinkling, rotate out of celery for at least a year, plow under or remove infected residue, and stay out of the bed when foliage is wet.

beginner: Seed is the main source, so start with tested, disease-free seed and clear away infected residue.
seasoned: Septoria-indexed seed is the single most important step; also remove or plow under infected debris.

beginner: Brown, water-soaked spots low on the stalks near the soil that turn into soft, mushy, rotted areas, sometimes covered in fluffy white mold with hard black specks in it. It rots the base of the plant, and plants short on calcium are hit hardest.
seasoned: Brown, water-soaked lesions develop on the petioles at or near the soil line and expand into soft, watery, decayed areas; in humid conditions a white cottony mold grows over them, later bearing hard black resting bodies (sclerotia) the size of small seeds. Plants weakened by calcium deficiency are especially susceptible. It is a rot of the dense, moist plant base rather than a leaf disease.

beginner: A soil fungus (Sclerotinia) that lives for years in the ground and attacks many plants. It thrives in cool, wet, crowded conditions where the base of the plant stays damp, so over-tight planting and overhead watering make it worse.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, which survives in soil as long-lived sclerotia and attacks many crops. It is favored by cool, wet conditions, prolonged leaf wetness, fog, dense canopies that stay damp, and overhead irrigation, which is why crowded, constantly wet celery is at greatest risk.

beginner: Move celery to a fresh spot each year, give plants enough room so air moves through and the bases dry out, water at the soil with drip instead of overhead, and keep calcium and watering steady so the plants are not weakened and easy to infect.
seasoned: Rotate away from celery and other susceptible crops to lower soil inoculum, space plants and rows for good airflow so the canopy and plant bases dry, use drip rather than sprinkler irrigation, avoid late-season overhead watering, and ensure adequate calcium and even moisture to keep plants from being predisposed.

beginner: Space plants and rows and water at the soil with drip so the dense plant base can dry. There is no home spray for pink rot.
seasoned: Open the canopy and switch from overhead to drip so the plant base dries; management is cultural, with no effective home fungicide.

beginner: The inside center of the plant, the youngest leaves and the growing tip, turns brown or black and dies, while the outer stalks can still look fine, so you often do not see it until you cut the plant open. Rot bacteria then move into the dead part and make it slimy and smelly.
seasoned: The young leaves and growing point in the center of the plant turn brown to black and die, while the outer stalks may still look healthy, so the damage is hidden until the plant is cut open. Secondary soft-rot bacteria often invade the dead tissue, producing a slimy, foul interior. It is a physiological disorder, not an infection, though it opens the door to one.

beginner: The growing center runs short of calcium. Usually the soil has enough, but the plant cannot move calcium to its fast-growing tip when watering is uneven, growth is too rushed, or the soil is too acidic. Celery is especially prone because it is shallow-rooted and needs so much water.
seasoned: A localized calcium deficiency in the fastest-growing tissue. It is usually not caused by truly calcium-poor soil but by anything that interrupts calcium delivery to the growing point: uneven or insufficient watering, rapid growth surges, high salts, or strongly acidic soil that limits calcium uptake. Celery's heavy water demand and shallow roots make it particularly prone.

beginner: The main fix is steady, even watering, never letting the soil swing from dry to soaked, because uneven water is what usually triggers it. Keep the soil pH in the right range so calcium stays available, do not push soft growth with too much nitrogen, and add calcium (like lime) only if a soil test shows you need it.
seasoned: The core prevention is even, uninterrupted moisture, since erratic watering is the usual trigger; keep soil pH in the recommended slightly acidic to neutral range so calcium stays available, avoid forcing soft, rapid growth with excessive nitrogen, and maintain adequate soil calcium where tests show it is low. Some growers find a calcium foliar spray to the developing heart helps under risky conditions.

beginner: Steady, even moisture is the core fix. Erratic watering is what starves the growing tip of calcium. Keep the soil pH in range so calcium stays available, and do not force soft growth with too much nitrogen.
seasoned: Uninterrupted moisture is the key lever, since erratic watering triggers the disorder; hold pH in the recommended range and avoid excess nitrogen that forces soft, rapid growth.

beginner: Celery needs more water, more steadily, than almost anything else in the garden. Keep the soil evenly damp all the time and never let it dry out. Give it at least 1 to 2 inches of water a week, counting rain, and more in hot weather or sandy soil. With celery, steady is the whole game.
seasoned: Celery is the thirstiest of the common garden vegetables and the least forgiving of a dry spell. It is shallow-rooted and descends from a marsh plant, so it wants the soil kept evenly and constantly moist, never swinging from dry to wet. Plan on at least 1 to 2 inches of water per week from rain or irrigation, and more in heat or on light soil, delivered often enough that the surface root zone never dries.

beginner: At least 1 to 2 inches a week, and more when it is hot or your soil is sandy. It is better to water a bit more often than to soak it once and let it dry out. A layer of mulch helps keep the soil damp.
seasoned: A minimum of 1 to 2 inches per week, increased in heat, wind, or fast-draining soil, applied frequently enough to avoid any dry-down. Mulch helps hold moisture and moderate soil temperature for the shallow roots.

beginner: Water at the soil with a drip line or soaker hose so the roots stay damp but the leaves and the crowded base of the plant stay dry. Wet leaves bring on the leaf-spot diseases and stalk rot, so avoid spraying the plants from overhead, especially in the evening.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose to keep the root zone constantly moist while keeping the foliage and the dense plant base dry, since wet leaves and a damp crown favor the leaf blights and pink rot. Avoid overhead sprinkling, especially late in the day and late in the season.

beginner: Soil that stays soaking wet, not just damp, can rot the base of the plant and turn the leaves yellow. You want steady moisture in rich soil that still drains, not a swamp. Mushy stalk bases and a sour, wet bed mean ease off.
seasoned: Constantly saturated, poorly drained soil invites pink rot and damping-off and yellows the foliage. The goal is steady moisture in well-amended, draining soil, not standing water; a sour, waterlogged bed and soft rotting stalk bases are the warning signs.

beginner: Letting celery go dry, even once, is the most common mistake. It makes the stalks stringy, tough, hollow, and bitter, and the damage does not undo itself. Droopy, dull leaves and stalled growth mean you waited too long, so keep the water steady rather than catching up after the fact.
seasoned: Even brief drought is the classic celery failure: the petioles turn stringy, tough, pithy or hollow, and bitter, and the plant may bolt under combined heat and water stress. Wilting, dull foliage and slow growth signal that the crop has already been checked, and the quality loss from a dry spell is not reversible.

beginner: Celery seeds are tiny and very slow to come up, so keep the surface of the mix damp the whole time. If it dries out even once, germination stalls.
seasoned: Celery seed is tiny, slow, and surface-sown, so keep the starting mix constantly and evenly moist through the long germination; never let the surface dry, which stalls the already slow, erratic sprouting.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp at all times. Celery comes from a marsh plant and never likes to dry out, even when small.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on with unbroken even moisture; celery is shallow-rooted and marsh-descended, and it has no slack period where it tolerates drying even as a young plant.

beginner: This is the make-or-break stretch, while the stalks fill out. Celery needs more water, more steadily, than almost anything in the garden: at least 1 to 2 inches a week, more when hot, and never let it dry out even briefly. Drying out now makes the stalks tough, stringy, and bitter, and you cannot fix it later. Water at the base and keep the leaves and crowded plant base dry.
seasoned: This is the long, punishing window: as the stalks form and bulk up, celery is the thirstiest of the common vegetables and the least forgiving of any dry-down. Keep the soil evenly and constantly moist, at least 1 to 2 inches a week and more in heat, applied often at the base with the canopy and crown kept dry against blight and pink rot. Any interruption turns the petioles stringy, pithy, and bitter, and it does not reverse.

beginner: Keep the same steady watering right up to harvest. A hot dry spell now can make celery bolt (run to seed), and letting it dry out still makes the stalks you pick tough and bitter.
seasoned: Hold the same constant, even moisture right through harvest; a heat-plus-drought stretch now can trigger bolting, and any dry-down still shows up directly in the eating quality of the stalks you cut.

beginner: Good celery comes down to keeping the roots evenly wet while keeping the leaves dry. Use a drip line or soaker hose and some mulch to hold the moisture, and avoid spraying the plants from above. Letting it dry out, even briefly, is what makes celery stringy and bitter, so do not rely on catching up later.
seasoned: The whole craft of growing good celery is steady water at the roots with a dry canopy. Use drip or a soaker hose and mulch to hold even moisture for the shallow roots, and keep overhead wetting off the foliage and crown to limit blight and pink rot. Any interruption shows up directly in the eating quality, so consistency matters more than volume.

beginner: Celery needs steady water its whole life, with no real break. The most important stretch is the long stretch while the stalks are filling out, when drying out makes them tough and bitter. Hot, dry spells are also dangerous because they can make celery bolt (run to seed). Basically, never let it get dry.
seasoned: Celery needs even moisture for its entire life, but two windows are most punishing to miss: the long establishment and bulking-up period when the stalks are forming, when any dry-down produces stringy, bitter petioles, and any heat-plus-drought stretch, which can trigger bolting. There is no slack period where celery tolerates drying.

beginner: Yes, harden celery off before transplanting, but do it by gradually reducing water rather than by exposing the plants to cold. Celery is unusual here: chilling the seedlings to toughen them can backfire and make them bolt later, so ease them outdoors over 7 to 10 days into mild, not cold, conditions.

Start celery indoors from seed, or buy young plants, because it is too slow to plant straight in the garden in most areas. Sow the seed about 8 to 10 weeks before you plan to set plants out. Barely cover the tiny seeds, since they need light and warmth (around 70°F) to sprout, and be patient, they can take 2 to 3 weeks. Plant out only after the risk of hard frost and long cold spells is over: cold-shocked young celery often bolts (runs to seed) later instead of making good stalks. Harden the plants off over a week or so by watering a little less, not by putting them out in the cold.
seasoned: Always start celery as a transplant; it is too slow and too long-season to direct sow in most of the country. Sow seed indoors about 8 to 10 weeks before the target transplant date, barely covering the fine seed (it needs light and warmth, ideally about 70°F, to germinate, and is slow, often 2 to 3 weeks). Grow the seedlings on and transplant out when they have several true leaves and, critically, only after the danger of a hard frost or a prolonged cold snap has passed: young celery exposed to roughly two or more weeks of temperatures near or below 50°F can vernalize and bolt later instead of forming usable stalks. Harden off over 7 to 10 days by easing water, not by chilling.

beginner: Celery does not need a deep pot because its roots are shallow, but it does need a pot big enough to stay damp. A container at least 8 inches deep works, but a bigger one (5 gallons or more) is much easier, because small pots dry out fast and celery hates drying out. A wide trough holding several plants is ideal.
seasoned: Celery is shallow-rooted, so depth is less critical than steady moisture and volume: a container at least 8 inches deep holds the roots, but a wider, larger pot (5 gallons or more) is far easier to keep evenly moist, which is the whole challenge. Group several plants in a roomy trough or half-barrel rather than single small pots, which dry too fast.

seasoned: A saucer can actually help here, because celery wants constant moisture: leaving a little water in the saucer between waterings buffers the pot against drying. Do not let it stand permanently full, though, since a constantly waterlogged mix invites pink rot and root rot.
